Receiving a job offer is exciting, but before you say "yes", take a few minutes to check the details.

1. Salary & Overtime
Make sure you understand your pay, overtime rates, and when you'll be paid.

Confirm your weekly hours, shift schedule, and whether weekend or night work is required.

Is the workplace easy to get to? If you're relocating, ask what support is available.

Check your holiday entitlement, pension, bonuses, and any additional company benefits.

Will you have opportunities to learn new skills and progress within the company?

The Psychology of Celebrating Our People: Why Every Work Anniversary Matters


As HR professionals, we often focus on performance, engagement, retention, and results. But there is another factor that deserves just as much attention: the emotional meaning of time.

When someone celebrates a work anniversary, we are not simply recognizing another year on a calendar. We are recognizing the moments behind it: the challenges overcome, the skills developed, the relationships built, and the contribution made to something larger than oneself.

From a psychological perspective, recognition reinforces a sense of belonging, purpose, and value. It tells people: Your time here has mattered. Your work has been seen. Your contribution has made a difference.

Celebrating our talent is not about creating a culture of constant praise. It is about creating moments of meaningful recognition—because people are more than their job titles or performance metrics. They are part of the story we are building together.

As HR professionals, we have the opportunity to make recognition intentional, authentic, and human.

Because when we celebrate someone’s journey, we are not only honoring their past—we are strengthening their connection to the future they are helping us build.

People remember how a company made them feel. Let’s make sure they feel that their time, effort, and contribution truly mattered.

In Ruli, Rwanda, miners haul 30-70 kg bags of tungsten out of tunnels for 10 to 50 cents a bag. 
Their entire work history lives as tick marks in a paper booklet.

Across Africa's informal economy, workers build skills and prove themselves for years. Then a job ends, and the record of it vanishes. 
That missing history shapes access to finance, insurance, and the next job.

Fixa is fixing this. 

They started as a labour contracting platform in Rwanda, supplying workers into construction. But every worker onboarded, every shift completed, every payroll run was quietly creating something that barely exists across the continent: verified employment data. 

So far, more than 20,000 digital employment identities, over 1 million shifts, and US$6 million in wages processed. Over 95% of their workers accessed earned wages for the first time in their lives.

What made us confident?
Plenty of platforms try to sell financial services into the informal economy before they've earned trust or built data. 
Fixa works the opposite way. Solve a real operational problem for employers first, build trusted employment records as a by-product, then use those records to unlock better services for workers.

We think every worker deserves to own a verified record of the work they've done. 

If that becomes part of Africa's labour market infrastructure, Fixa will have helped build it.

Today's infrastructure projects become tomorrow's hiring announcements.

The airport and technology center already support more than 150 companies, and county leaders are positioning the area to attract additional:
Aviation and aerospace companies
Advanced manufacturers
Logistics and distribution operations
Industrial and technology businesses
While no official job numbers have been announced for this latest infrastructure project, previous airport expansions have included new hangars and additional full-time positions—and this investment is designed to create the conditions for more growth.

As our region grows, we shouldn't wait until employers start hiring.
We should be asking:
Do we have enough skilled workers?
Are local students aware of these career paths?
Are training providers preparing people for these industries?
Are employers connected to the workforce resources already available?
Those conversations should happen now—not after a company announces it's hiring.

✅ Moving faster through recruitment processes
✅ Investing in succession planning
✅ Offering flexible working arrangements
✅ Clearly communicating career development opportunities and organisational purpose.

Reposting this because the upcoming changes to unfair dismissal protection will make one thing increasingly important: what happens in the first six months of employment. 🙌🏼

A situation I have seen more than once:

“We need to dismiss them.”

Okay. What happened?

“Well… they’ve been struggling for a while.”

How long is “a while”?

“About four months.”

Excellent. And what feedback have they had?

“Not much.”

Right.

And what was discussed at probation?

“Nothing formal.”

At this point, HR is expected to perform an employment law exorcism and fix six months of poor management in one meeting.

The better approach starts much earlier.

Before the employee starts:
→ Is the role and expectation clear?

During onboarding:
→ Are they actually being set up to succeed?

At probation:
→ Is there an honest assessment of performance and fit?

When concerns arise:
→ Are they being addressed early, clearly and consistently?

That is where my experience across Talent Acquisition and HR has been particularly valuable.

The recruitment decision is only the beginning. If the process from “we want to hire them” to “we need to dismiss them” is disconnected, the problem is usually not created at the end.

It has been quietly accumulating for months.

The upcoming changes make getting that process right even more important.

And, ideally, mean fewer meetings beginning with: “We need to get rid of them” and ending with everyone looking at HR as though we have a magic wand. (Newsflash, we don’t) 👀

By Lisa Matomola

A key part of our consulting work at Hito HR involves helping organisations attract and hire the right people.

While recruitment may appear straightforward, the reality is often far more complex, particularly for organisations operating within tight budgets.

One lesson has become increasingly clear over the years: Talent is not cheap. Neither is hiring the wrong person.

Whenever I hear concerns about salary expectations, I encourage employers to pause and look beyond the number on the offer letter. Instead of asking, "Can we afford this candidate?" I ask a different question: "Can you afford not to hire them?"

That question often changes the entire conversation.

A few thousand dollars may seem like a significant amount during salary negotiations, but what will it cost if the position remains vacant for another six months? What will it cost if critical projects are delayed because no one has the expertise to lead them?
